radar.title: Spreading Dynamics on Higher-Order Networks: A Structure-Mechanism-Behavior Perspective with Applications
radar.summary: Spreading in real-world networks, including modern communication and networked systems, often unfolds through group interactions rather than isolated pairwise contacts. Higher-order network representations such as simplicial complexes, hypergraphs, and their temporal, multilayer, and directed extensions provide a principled way to encode group interactions. Unfortunately, existing studies on spreading over these substrates remain fragmented and largely model-centric, offering limited insight into how higher-order representations and contagion mechanisms jointly shape emergent dynamics. This review addresses this gap by introducing a structure-mechanism-behavior three-level perspective that provides a systematic mapping from higher-order network structures and spreading mechanisms to collective behaviors. Within this framework, we compare how different higher-order network representations encode group interactions, introduce a taxonomy of contagion mechanisms, and analyze their structural carrying capacity, defined as the ability of a given representation to support specific contagion mechanisms and the associated dynamical behaviors. We further map specific structure-mechanism combinations to three hallmark emergent behaviors, thereby offering a unified cross-level perspective beyond existing model-centric surveys. These insights are particularly relevant for communication systems involving group interactions, such as social information spreading, cooperative protocols, and distributed networked processes. Lastly, leveraging this three-level perspective, we offer a roadmap for guiding and controlling dynamics on higher-order networks, while discussing future directions in representation choice, mechanism design, and data-driven inference.

radar.title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty
radar.summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.

radar.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

radar.title: Posterior-conditioned multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive cyber defense
radar.summary: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. In addition to its local history, each defender conditions its decentralized policy on a shared attack-context belief, a probabilistic representation of the attack regime inferred online from recent multi-agent interaction trajectories. This belief provides a low-dimensional representation of evolving adversarial behavior and enables coordinated adaptation during execution without test-time policy optimization or retraining. We provide a performance analysis that quantifies how errors in the inferred attack-context belief translate into degraded long-term defense performance, clarifying the tradeoff between robustness and adaptivity. radar.title: Dynamic Contract Design with Learning
radar.summary: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable. In “Dynamic Contract Design with Learning,” Wang, Liang, and Sun study the interaction between learning and moral hazard: effort is costly and unobservable, so a missing arrival may reflect an unfavorable market, bad luck, or shirking. The firm’s goal is to design a dynamic contract governing arrival-based payments and termination, thereby motivating effort while learning whether to continue. Yet shirking can make the principal more pessimistic than the agent and create scope to manipulate future payments. The authors prove that an optimal contract inducing full effort until termination exists, but computing it appears prohibitively complex. They develop two simple online contracts with payments and termination thresholds fixed in advance. Both induce full effort and achieve O(ln T) regret over T periods against a first-best, full-information benchmark. A matching Ω(ln T) lower bound proves rate optimality. The results extend to continuous time and differing prior beliefs.
radar.summary_short: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable.

radar.title: Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Agent-to-Agent Communication Architecture for the Agentic Web
radar.summary: The Agentic Web needs to support continuous collaboration among agents from different organizations. These collaborative relationships may span multiple tasks, network connections and execution instances. Such interactions require stable communication entries, message reception when instances are offline, and source verification after delayed reading. How to organize these responsibilities so that cross domain communication does not depend on specific execution instances being continuously online is a key issue for building long term agent interaction infrastructure. We propose ATP (Agent Transfer Protocol), a cross organization agent communication protocol adopting a domain mediated architecture. In this architecture, administrative domains maintain stable addresses and receiving entries for logical agents. The domain servers of both parties continuously undertake cross domain transmission. The receiving domain verifies and saves messages for execution instances to read later. The sending domain signs the complete message envelope. This allows the receiving instance to independently reverify the domain source and content integrity after the original connection ends, provided the original verification public key is still trusted and obtainable. We implemented an ATP prototype and evaluated it through a controlled cross organization LLM agent workflow, mechanism checks and latency measurements. The workflow completed subsequent business processing after instances went offline or were replaced. The independent verifier successfully verified the domain source and content integrity of saved messages. Latency measurements further quantified the communication and processing overhead introduced by the continuous mediation of domain servers.
radar.summary_short: The Agentic Web needs to support continuous collaboration among agents from different organizations. These collaborative relationships may span multiple tasks, network connections and execution instances.

radar.title: Vision-Based Density Estimation for Adaptive Traffic Control
radar.summary: Traffic congestion is becoming a critical challenge in rapidly growing urban centers, particularly in developing nations where rapid urbanization and inadequate transport infrastructure place increasing strain on transport networks. In highly heterogeneous and chaotic traffic flows, camera-based traffic-state estimation is limited by severe vehicle occlusion and overlap. In this paper, we propose a framework to optimize traffic flow directly from stochastic visual observations. The architecture is structurally decoupled into three primary components: (a) vehicle density estimation, (b) predictive dynamics modeling, and (c) policy optimization. The proposed methodology introduces a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the mapping from camera feeds to spatial density maps, utilizing an adaptive k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) Gaussian kernel to handle varying congestion levels. This feeds into an ST3DNet predictive module for spatiotemporal forecasting, followed by a hierarchical Graph-Transformer Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithm to optimize signal phases. The density estimation stage was evaluated on 40 annotated intersection images from Rambagh 4, Jaipur, India, with a reported five-fold validation mean absolute error (MAE) of $3.32 \pm 0.95$ vehicles and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 14.5%. These results pertain to the perception component; empirical training and evaluation of the forecasting and control stages remain future work.
radar.summary_short: Traffic congestion is becoming a critical challenge in rapidly growing urban centers, particularly in developing nations where rapid urbanization and inadequate transport infrastructure place increasing strain on transport networks.

radar.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
radar.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
